title: Whispers from the Neighbors: Rethinking Caption Consensus as Inference-Time Evidence for Vision-Language Retrieval

paper.title: Whispers from the Neighbors: Rethinking Caption Consensus as Inference-Time Evidence for Vision-Language Retrieval
paper.abstract: Abstract An image is rarely described only once. Retrieval benchmarks and many collections attach several captions to each picture, yet dual encoders still judge every image-caption pair in isolation. We ask what these neighboring captions contribute when a frozen encoder consults them at inference time. Fusing image similarity with similarity to an image’s own captions improves text-to-image R@1 by 3.4 to 16.8 points across nine frozen encoders when the captions come from the same annotators as the queries. The gain falls to 1.9 to 7.2 points when an off-the-shelf captioner writes them, and to at most one point when they come from a different annotation source; a paraphrase-trained text encoder strengthens the text side further. A natural refinement, scoring the part of the image that the captions leave unexplained, appears to add much more under a leave-one-out evaluation. We show that this advantage arises because the correct candidate’s supports are built differently from those of the negative candidates, with set size and query removal each contributing about half, and that under a fixed support index the residual reduces to a reweighting of what the captions already provide. On compositional benchmarks, the captions help by matching candidates to human descriptions of the image, without improving image-text grounding. The code is available at: https://github.com/nhatkhangcs/clip_consensus

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Dual encoders such as CLIP ( Radford et al., 2021 ) and SigLIP ( Zhai et al., 2023 ) map images and text into a shared embedding space and retrieve by cosine similarity. This simple design supports zero-shot classification and image-text retrieval at scale, and later work has improved it through alternative losses, data curation, and scaling ( Cherti et al., 2023 ; Xu et al., 2024 ; Gadre et al., 2023 ; Fang et al., 2024 ; Sun et al., 2023 ) . At retrieval time, however, each image is still represented by a single vector, and each image-caption pair is scored in isolation. Many image collections offer more than the image itself. COCO and Flickr30K attach five human captions to every image ( Lin et al., 2014 ; Young et al., 2014 ) , and curated repositories often store alt text, descriptions, or other metadata alongside each picture. These captions describe overlapping but non-identical aspects of the scene: some content is mentioned by every annotator, while other details appear in only one caption ( Plummer et al., 2017 ) . Standard image-text benchmarks use them as queries or training targets, but not as evidence when a candidate image is scored. Figure 1: With image similarity alone, the query is closest to a distractor. Adding the consensus of the correct image’s own captions recovers the correct match. Figure 1 illustrates why these captions can help. For the query “A person in a grass field flying a kite,” image similarity alone prefers a photo of a person reaching for a Frisbee in tall grass, whereas the captions of the correct image, which describe people flying kites on a lawn, lie much closer to the query than its image embedding does. Using candidate-side text in this way is a form of database-side augmentation and late fusion, long used in instance retrieval ( Chum et al., 2007 ; Arandjelović and Zisserman, 2012 ) , document expansion ( Nogueira et al., 2019 ) , and retrieval over multimodal candidates ( Wei et al., 2024 ) . We do not propose it as a new method. Instead, we ask how much it actually helps frozen dual encoders, and how to evaluate it without leakage. We study a simple scorer: the support captions of each candidate image are averaged into a consensus direction, the image embedding is decomposed into a component along this direction and a residual, and the query is scored by a weighted sum of image, consensus, and residual similarity, with only two fusion weights tuned. Evaluating such a scorer requires care. In multi-caption benchmarks, the query is usually one of the correct image’s own captions, so it must be excluded from that image’s supports. A natural remedy, leave-one-out (LOO), removes the query from the correct candidate only. Under LOO, the full scorer outperforms a tuned base-plus-consensus scorer by 5.3 to 8.1 points in image-to-text R@1 on COCO. Under a fixed support index, in which every candidate uses the same supports regardless of the query, this advantage falls to at most 0.7 points. A size-matched variant of LOO, in which every negative also drops one caption, recovers about half of the gap, so set size and query removal each account for roughly half of the inflation. The support captions themselves, however, help every encoder we evaluate. Our contributions are as follows. • A leakage-free protocol. We evaluate candidate-side captions under a fixed support index, with every scorer tuned on the same objective and image-clustered bootstrap intervals, and release it as a standalone evaluation script. • An account of the LOO pitfall. We show that LOO inflates the apparent benefit of a residual term derived from the same captions. A size-matched LOO, a random-support control, and an algebraic analysis show that the residual reduces to a candidate-dependent reweighting of image and consensus similarity, which yields at most a small text-to-image gain. • Measurements of when candidate-side text helps. Text-to-image R@1 improves by 3.4 to 16.8 points with same-source human captions across nine frozen encoders, by 1.9 to 7.2 points with captions from an off-the-shelf captioner across six, and by at most one point with captions from a different annotation source across four. A paraphrase-trained text encoder strengthens the text side, the gains persist under corrected COCO positives, and on SugarCrepe and ARO they come from text-to-text matching against human descriptions of the image, not from better image-text grounding.

sections.heading: Image-text dual encoders.
sections.text: CLIP and ALIGN train dual encoders to align matched image-caption pairs in a shared embedding space, enabling zero-shot classification and image-text retrieval ( Radford et al., 2021 ; Jia et al., 2021 ) . Later work improves this recipe through scaling ( Cherti et al., 2023 ) , the pairwise sigmoid loss of SigLIP ( Zhai et al., 2023 ; Tschannen et al., 2025 ) , data curation in MetaCLIP, DataComp, and DFN ( Xu et al., 2024 ; Gadre et al., 2023 ; Fang et al., 2024 ) , and improved training as in EVA-CLIP ( Sun et al., 2023 ) . Retrieval has also been improved with hard negatives ( Faghri et al., 2018 ) , region-word or token-level interaction ( Lee et al., 2018 ; Yao et al., 2022 ) , and fusion or generative pre-training ( Li et al., 2021 ; Li et al., 2022 ; Li et al., 2023a ; Yu et al., 2022 ) . A related line questions the one-to-one image-caption assumption during training, through multiple positives ( Bulat et al., 2024 ) , generated captions ( Wang et al., 2025 ) , richer image representations ( Lavoie et al., 2024 ) , or objectives that capture more than shared information ( Dufumier et al., 2025 ) . All of these change training; we keep the encoder frozen and change only how candidates are scored.

sections.heading: Candidate-side text and late fusion.
sections.text: Augmenting each database item with related content is an established retrieval technique. In instance retrieval, average query expansion and database-side augmentation replace an item’s descriptor with the mean of its neighbors ( Chum et al., 2007 ; Arandjelović and Zisserman, 2012 ) ; in text retrieval, document expansion appends predicted queries to each document ( Nogueira et al., 2019 ) . Benchmarks with multimodal candidates, such as M-BEIR, score image-text pairs by fusing image and text similarities ( Wei et al., 2024 ) , and ECO re-ranks captions of a fixed image by their agreement with other captions ( Jeong et al., 2024 ) . The scorer we study applies the same idea to frozen vision-language retrieval, with each candidate’s own captions as the added text. Our focus is therefore not the fusion itself but how much it helps, which text encoder suits the text side, from sparse BM25 ( Robertson and Zaragoza, 2009 ) to sentence encoders ( Reimers and Gurevych, 2019 ; Wang et al., 2022 ; Li et al., 2023b ) , and how to evaluate it without leakage.

sections.heading: Inference-time score normalization.
sections.text: Cross-modal retrieval can also be improved at inference time without any metadata, by normalizing scores against other queries. Inverted softmax ( Smith et al., 2017 ) and dual softmax ( Cheng et al., 2021 ) renormalize over the evaluated query set, and QB-Norm uses a separate query bank to reduce hubness ( Bogolin et al., 2022 ) . We compare against these methods to separate gains that require captions from gains that any normalization provides.

sections.heading: Evaluation of image-text retrieval.
sections.text: COCO and Flickr30K pair each image with five captions ( Lin et al., 2014 ; Young et al., 2014 ) , and Flickr30K Entities links entity mentions across them ( Plummer et al., 2017 ) ; Localized Narratives add a second, independent description of the same images ( Pont-Tuset et al., 2020 ) . Single-positive COCO evaluation misses many valid matches, which CxC and ECCV Caption correct with additional human and machine-verified positives ( Parekh et al., 2021 ; Chun et al., 2022 ) . Compositional benchmarks such as Winoground, ARO, CREPE, and SugarCrepe test whether models distinguish captions with the same words in different structures ( Thrush et al., 2022 ; Yuksekgonul et al., 2023 ; Ma et al., 2023 ; Hsieh et al., 2023 ) ; Hsieh et al. (2023) show that blind text models solve many earlier benchmarks. We follow this concern and pair every compositional result with blind baselines that never see the image.

sections.heading: 3 Methodology
sections.text: Figure 2: Overview of the consensus-residual scorer. For a candidate image, the support captions are averaged into a consensus direction, the image embedding is split into a component along this direction and a residual, and the query is scored against the image, the consensus, and the residual. Section 4.2 shows that, under a fixed support index, the residual path contributes little beyond the consensus path. We consider image-text retrieval in which each database image is accompanied by several natural captions. Using a frozen dual encoder, we encode the image and its support captions, average the captions into a consensus direction, split the image embedding relative to this direction, and combine base, consensus, and residual similarity (Figure 2 ). Section 4.2 analyzes what each term contributes.

sections.heading: 3.5 Support Construction for Evaluation
sections.text: Figure 3: Three ways to exclude the query ( ⋆ \star ) from the supports. Leave-one-out removes it from the positive only, so the positive’s support set differs from the negatives’ in both size and content. Size-matched LOO equalizes the size by dropping a random caption from each negative. The fixed support index holds out the same caption slot for every image, so support sets do not depend on the query. In multi-caption benchmarks, a query caption is usually one of the captions of its positive image, T q = T i , m T_{q}=T_{i,m} . If the query remains in that image’s support set, it is compared with an average that contains itself, which leaks the answer. We consider three constructions that avoid this leakage (Figure 3 ).

sections.heading: Leave-one-out (LOO).
sections.text: A natural first choice removes the query from the positive candidate only: the positive uses 𝐜 i , − m \mathbf{c}_{i,-m} , the normalized mean of { 𝐭 i , n } n ≠ m \{\mathbf{t}_{i,n}\}_{n\neq m} , and the corresponding residual 𝐩 ^ i , − m \hat{\mathbf{p}}_{i,-m} , while every negative candidate keeps all K K captions. This removes self-similarity, but the support set of the positive now differs from those of the negatives in both size and content, and building it requires knowing which candidate is the positive.

sections.heading: Size-matched LOO.
sections.text: To separate these two differences, we also evaluate a variant in which every negative drops one randomly chosen caption, so that all candidates have K − 1 K-1 supports while the positive still excludes the query specifically. We use it only as a diagnostic (Section 4.2 ).

sections.heading: Fixed support index.
sections.text: One caption per image is held out as the query across the entire database, and every candidate uses its remaining K − 1 K-1 captions. With K = 5 K=5 , fold f ∈ { 1 , … , 5 } f\in\{1,\dots,5\} holds out caption f f of every image, and results are averaged over folds. Support sets therefore do not depend on the query, as in a deployed system in which unseen queries are matched against a fixed index. We use the fixed support index for all main results and report the two LOO variants only for comparison (Section 4.2 ). When supports come from a different source than the queries, such as captions generated by a captioning model or Localized Narratives (Section 4.4 ), no query can appear among the supports, and all human captions serve as queries. In image-to-text retrieval under the fixed index, the consensus is built from the query image’s own remaining captions and each query has a single correct caption, so we treat these results as diagnostic and report them in Appendix B.1 .

sections.heading: 4 Experiments
sections.text: We first measure what support captions add under a fixed support index (§ 4.1 ) and analyze the residual term (§ 4.2 ). We then examine the text side and metadata-free alternatives (§ 4.3 ), the source of the supports (§ 4.4 ), and compositional benchmarks (§ 4.5 ). Success and failure cases are in Appendix I .

sections.heading: Encoders and splits.
sections.text: We use six frozen dual encoders: OpenCLIP ViT-B/32 ( Cherti et al., 2023 ) , MetaCLIP ViT-B/16 ( Xu et al., 2024 ) , DFN ViT-B/16 ( Fang et al., 2024 ) , DataComp ViT-B/32 ( Gadre et al., 2023 ) , EVA02 ViT-B/16 ( Sun et al., 2023 ) , and SigLIP ViT-B/16 ( Zhai et al., 2023 ) . Appendix H.1 repeats the main experiments on three further encoders, SigLIP2 ViT-B/16, SigLIP2 So400m/14 ( Tschannen et al., 2025 ) , and CLIP ViT-L/14 ( Radford et al., 2021 ) ; together these are the nine frozen encoders of the abstract, and the fine-tuned BLIP-2 is reported separately. We split the Karpathy COCO test set ( Karpathy and Fei-Fei, 2015 ) into tune2500 (the first 2,500 images) and eval2500 (the remaining 2,500). All weights are selected on tune2500, and we report results on eval2500 and on Flickr30K test1k, which serves as a held-out transfer setting.

sections.heading: Scorers, protocols, and statistics.
sections.text: We compare Base , B+C , and Full (Section 3 ), each tuned by grid search on tune2500 with α = 1 \alpha=1 and the objective I2T@1 + T2I@1, separately for each encoder, scorer, and protocol; every baseline below is tuned the same way. Since the encoders stay frozen while two weights are fit on labeled data, we describe the scorer as encoder-frozen . Unless noted otherwise, results use the fixed support index of Section 3.5 , averaged over five folds. Under this index T2I@1 coincides with standard T2I@1, while I2T@1 has a single correct caption per query, so we report fixed-index I2T only as a diagnostic (Appendix B.1 ). Differences carry 95% confidence intervals from a paired bootstrap over whole images (1,000 resamples). All experiments run on a single 40 GB GPU; search grids, tuned weights, and implementation details are in Appendix A.1 .

sections.heading: Effect of the evaluation protocol.
sections.text: Table 2 contrasts Full with a separately tuned B+C under the three constructions of Section 3.5 . Under standard LOO, Full leads B+C by 5.3 to 8.1 I2T@1 points on COCO and by 2.6 to 3.4 on Flickr30K, with every interval excluding zero. Under the fixed support index, the lead never exceeds 0.7 points. Size-matched LOO, in which every negative also drops one caption, lies in between, at 2.6 to 4.6 points on COCO and 0.4 to 1.4 on Flickr30K. Equalizing set size therefore removes roughly half of the inflation on COCO and half or more on Flickr30K. The remainder comes from the positive’s supports excluding the query specifically: the LOO residual of the positive keeps a small positive projection onto the query (0.009 to 0.034 on average), whereas residuals computed from other captions of the same image have none on average. A random-support control on SigLIP and CLIP ViT-L/14 confirms that the LOO gain requires supports that both exclude the query and describe the image (Appendix C.2 ).

In I2T, the query image fixes s i s_{i} , so within each query Full ranks candidates exactly as B+C would with a query-specific consensus weight. In T2I, s i s_{i} varies across candidates, and the residual acts as a per-image consensus weight, which matches its small T2I gains under the fixed index. On four encoders, residuals that cannot be written in this form, and reliability-weighted consensus, improve on B+C by at most 0.86 points (Appendix C.4 ).

sections.heading: Metadata-free normalization.
sections.text: Part of any inference-time gain could come from correcting hubness, not from the captions themselves. QB-Norm ( Bogolin et al., 2022 ) , with a query bank disjoint from the evaluated queries, improves COCO T2I@1 by 1.7 to 2.1 points and slightly hurts Flickr30K (Table 3 ), far below the gain from supports. Inverted and dual softmax ( Smith et al., 2017 ; Cheng et al., 2021 ) gain 7.4 to 10.0 T2I@1 points, but they normalize over the full set of evaluated queries and exploit the one-query-per-image structure of this protocol, so we treat them as transductive references (Appendix D.2 ). Most of the support gain is therefore specific to the captions.

sections.heading: A stronger text side.
sections.text: B+C scores the supports with the encoder’s own text tower, which is not trained for paraphrase similarity. Replacing it with a sentence encoder changes the picture. GTE-large ( Li et al., 2023b ) over the four supports alone reaches 54.7 COCO T2I@1, comparable to the image-only Base of the strongest encoder, and fusing it with the image score beats B+C on every encoder and dataset, by 2.6 to 4.3 T2I@1 points and 3.1 to 7.6 I2T@1 points, with every interval excluding zero. BM25 ( Robertson and Zaragoza, 2009 ) is a much weaker text side and falls below B+C in T2I on 11 of the 12 encoder–dataset pairs. The fusion also exceeds both of its parts, so combining modalities remains essential; what B+C leaves on the table is the quality of the text encoder. E5 and MPNet reach text-only accuracy close to GTE (Appendix D.1 ).

sections.heading: Generated supports.
sections.text: Multiple human captions per image are rare outside COCO and Flickr30K, so we replace them with four captions per image generated by Qwen2.5-VL-3B ( Bai et al., 2025 ) . No query can then appear among the supports, and image-to-text R@1 is the standard 5-positive metric. Generated supports improve every encoder in both directions (Table 4 ), by 1.9 to 7.2 T2I@1 and 1.9 to 7.3 I2T@1 points, recovering 42 to 59% of the COCO T2I gain obtained with human supports. Generated captions alone retrieve worse than the image alone on every encoder, so the gain again comes from the combination. Because the captioner is itself a strong vision model, part of this gain may transfer its visual knowledge.

sections.heading: Cross-source human supports.
sections.text: To remove same-source paraphrasing, we pair queries and supports from different annotation sources using Localized Narratives ( Pont-Tuset et al., 2020 ) , on SigLIP and the three encoders of Appendix H.1 . With human captions as queries and a single narrative as support, B+C gains at most 1.0 point, and tuning switches the support term off for both SigLIP2 encoders (Appendix E.2 ). Support captions are thus most valuable when they share the distribution of the queries.

sections.heading: Number and quality of supports.
sections.text: The benefit of the captions grows with their number and falls with their quality (Figure 4 ). With a single support per image, B+C is at or below Base for the three SigLIP encoders, and the gain rises steadily up to four supports (Appendix B.4 ). We also replace a fraction of each image’s supports with captions of other images, never with query captions (Appendix E.3 ). With weights fixed at their clean values, the gain becomes negative at 60% mismatch ( − 1.6 -1.6 for SigLIP and − 4.2 -4.2 for OpenCLIP). Retuned weights stay at or above Base at every level, because tuning shifts weight back to the image; for SigLIP, it also switches the residual off at 60%. Fusion weights should therefore be calibrated to the expected support quality. Figure 4: Text-to-image R@1 gain of B+C over Base on COCO. (a) Number of supports per image, with weights tuned for four supports. (b) Fraction of supports replaced by captions of other images, with weights kept at their clean values (dashed) or retuned at each replacement level (solid).

sections.heading: Stronger models.
sections.text: For SigLIP2 So400m, the strongest frozen encoder we test, B+C still adds 3.4 to 3.5 T2I@1 points (Appendix H.1 ). For BLIP-2 ViT-g fine-tuned on COCO ( Li et al., 2023a ) , adding the consensus term after ITM re-ranking of the top 16 candidates gains 0.9 to 1.1 T2I@1 points, and a per-token residual adds a further 0.2 to 0.4 points, significant only on Flickr30K (Appendix F ).

sections.heading: 4.6 Qualitative Analysis
sections.text: Over all 12,500 COCO eval2500 queries, Full with SigLIP ViT-B/16 moves 1,069 text-to-image queries from an incorrect to a correct top-1 relative to Base, and 392 the other way. Figure 5 shows randomly drawn examples of the first kind. The distractors that Base prefers share the broad content of the query but miss a specific detail: a sandwich with meat instead of a vegetable sandwich, or a desk with one monitor instead of two. The captions of the correct image tend to name exactly these details (“a vegetable sandwich sits on a paper plate”, “the computer desk has two monitors”), so the consensus term favors it even when its image embedding lies slightly farther from the query. The failures follow the opposite pattern (Appendix I ). Their queries are generic, several images fit them equally well, and a distractor’s captions agree with the query as closely as those of the correct image. Many of these errors are false negatives of single-positive evaluation, consistent with the gains under CxC and ECCV Caption (Section 4.1 ). Figure 5: Text-to-image queries where support captions correct the ranking, drawn at random from all such queries. Each panel shows the top three images for one query under Base (top row) and Full (bottom row); green marks the correct image, which moves from rank 2 or 3 to rank 1.

sections.heading: 5 Discussion and Recommendations
sections.text: Our results suggest several practices for work that conditions retrieval on text attached to candidates.

sections.heading: Make support sets independent of the query.
sections.text: Any construction that treats the positive candidate differently from the negatives can inflate a scorer’s apparent benefit. Leave-one-out differs in both set size and content, and the image-to-text gain of 5.3 to 8.1 points it produces shrinks to at most 0.7 points under a fixed support index. Where LOO cannot be avoided, a size-matched variant at least removes the set-size effect.

sections.heading: Compare new terms against tuned simpler scorers.
sections.text: The residual term looked essential until base-plus-consensus was tuned under the same protocol and objective. Its algebraic form then explained why: it only reweights similarities that the simpler scorer already uses. Each ablated variant should therefore be retuned, not evaluated with the weights of the full model.

sections.heading: Choose the text side deliberately.
sections.text: A dual encoder’s own text tower is not trained for paraphrase similarity, and a sentence encoder over the same captions outperformed it for all six encoders. Which encoder reads the supports is a design decision in its own right, not a detail inherited from the image model.

sections.heading: Report where the supports come from.
sections.text: How much the supports help depends on how closely they resemble the queries. Same-source human captions give the largest gains, generated captions recover part of them, and captions from another annotation source add almost nothing. A result obtained with same-source supports therefore overstates what to expect in deployment, where queries and metadata are seldom written alike.

sections.heading: Calibrate to support quality.
sections.text: Weights tuned on clean supports can push retrieval below the image-only baseline when supports are noisy, whereas in our tests weights retuned for the noise level kept it at or above Base. Fusion weights should match the support quality expected at deployment.

sections.heading: Pair compositional results with blind baselines.
sections.text: A language model that never sees the image solves ARO-Order, so improvements on it say nothing about grounding. Reporting blind and random-support references next to any scorer that uses text shows what a gain actually measures.

sections.heading: 6 Conclusion
sections.text: We asked how much the captions attached to database images help frozen dual encoders at retrieval time, and how to measure it without leakage. Under a fixed support index, fusing image similarity with similarity to an image’s own captions improves text-to-image R@1 for every encoder we tested. The gain is largest when the captions share an annotation source with the queries, about half as large when an off-the-shelf captioner writes them, and close to zero when they come from a different source. The text encoder deserves as much care as the fusion: a paraphrase-trained sentence encoder over the same captions outperforms each dual encoder’s own text tower. The residual term that motivated our decomposition adds little. Its large image-to-text advantage under leave-one-out evaluation arises because the positive’s supports are built differently from those of the negatives, with set size and query removal each explaining part of the gap; under a fixed index, it reduces to a reweighting of image and consensus similarity. On compositional benchmarks, the gains come from matching candidates against human descriptions of the image, not from better grounding, and ARO can be solved without the image. We release the fixed-support-index protocol so that future work on candidate-side text can be compared on equal terms.

sections.heading: Limitations
sections.text: Our setting assumes that each database image comes with descriptive text. We evaluate human captions from COCO and Flickr30K, Localized Narratives, and captions generated by Qwen2.5-VL, but not naturally occurring metadata such as alt text, Wikipedia descriptions, or product titles, whose relation to the queries may differ. Because the scorer sees text that image-only retrieval does not, comparisons with Base measure the value of that text, not an improvement of the encoder. The fusion weights are tuned on labeled COCO images. They transfer to Flickr30K, but both datasets consist of short, crowd-sourced English captions written under similar guidelines, and we have not evaluated other languages or domains. With generated supports, the captioner is itself a strong vision model, so part of the gain may stem from its visual knowledge and not from the text alone. The gains shrink as the base model becomes stronger, to about one point for BLIP-2 with ITM re-ranking, and they decrease with fewer supports per image (Appendix B.4 ). Under the fixed support index, image-to-text R@1 has a single correct caption per query and is not comparable to standard five-positive results, so we treat it as a diagnostic. Several analyses (cross-source supports, fusion rules, residual variants, and the random-support control) were run on a subset of encoders. Finally, ARO can be solved by a blind language model, so among our compositional benchmarks only SugarCrepe speaks to grounding, and there the captions help through text matching instead of through the image.

sections.heading: Fixed support index.
sections.text: In fold f ∈ { 1 , … , 5 } f\in\{1,\dots,5\} , caption f f of every image is the query, and every candidate image keeps its remaining four captions as supports. Candidates are therefore scored against support sets that do not depend on the query. We report the mean over folds and, where noted, the standard deviation. In I2T, each image query has one correct caption, compared with five in standard 5K I2T, so absolute I2T@1 values are lower than standard numbers (SigLIP Base on COCO: 54.96 vs. 73.44). In T2I, the fold average equals standard T2I@1, since every caption is a query exactly once (SigLIP: 54.60 on COCO and 74.60 on Flickr30K; CLIP ViT-L/14: 43.77 on COCO, identical under both protocols). Fold standard deviations are much larger on Flickr30K ( ± \pm 4–8) than on COCO ( ± \pm 0.5–1.8), because caption position in the Flickr30K Karpathy file is not random (Appendix B.3 ). All paired comparisons use the same folds, so this variation largely cancels in Δ \Delta .

sections.heading: Leave-one-out (LOO).
sections.text: Every caption is a query. The positive image drops the query from its supports (four captions), while each negative keeps all five of its captions.

sections.heading: Splits.
sections.text: COCO tune2500 and eval2500 are images 0–2499 and 2500–4999 of the Karpathy 5K test split. Flickr30K test1k is the Karpathy test split. No weights are tuned on eval2500 or Flickr30K.

sections.heading: Implementation details.
sections.text: All encoders are used off the shelf and never updated. Image and caption embeddings are computed once, stored in fp32, and ℓ 2 \ell_{2} -normalized; all scores are dot products of these embeddings. The method has no trainable parameters beyond the fusion weights β \beta and γ \gamma , and α = 1 \alpha=1 throughout.

sections.heading: Tuning.

sections.heading: A.2 Practical Cost
sections.text: For frozen dual encoders, B+C and Full are linear in the query: s ⁡ ( I i , T q ) = 𝐭 q ⊤ ​ 𝐮 i s(I_{i},T_{q})=\mathbf{t}_{q}^{\top}\mathbf{u}_{i} with 𝐮 i = α ​ 𝐯 i + β ​ 𝐜 i + γ ​ 𝐩 ^ i \mathbf{u}_{i}=\alpha\mathbf{v}_{i}+\beta\mathbf{c}_{i}+\gamma\hat{\mathbf{p}}_{i} . Each image is therefore indexed by one precomputed vector of the same size as its image embedding, and ranking with 𝐮 i \mathbf{u}_{i} reproduces Full’s top-1 on all 12,500 COCO eval2500 queries (score differences below 10 − 6 10^{-6} ). On a GPU with one million 768-dimensional images in fp16, the index occupies 1.54 GB for both Base and Full, building all 𝐮 i \mathbf{u}_{i} from four supports takes 0.09 s, and a single query takes 1.21 ms (Base) versus 1.20 ms (Full). The per-token BLIP-2 variant is not linear and must store the residual of each query token, or recompute it from the consensus at query time. Unlike B+C and Full, which fold into one precomputed vector per image and keep the index size of Base (Appendix A.2 ), the per-token variant must store a residual for every query token or recompute it at query time.

sections.heading: Appendix I Qualitative Results
sections.text: Figures 5 and 6 show text-to-image retrieval on COCO eval2500 under the fixed support index. For each query, we show the top three images retrieved by Base and by Full; the correct image is framed in green and the others in red. Here Full is the consensus–residual scorer with SigLIP ViT-B/16 and the fixed-protocol weights tuned on COCO tune2500 ( β = 0.3 \beta=0.3 , γ = 0.6 \gamma=0.6 ). Over all 12,500 queries, Full moves 1,069 queries from an incorrect to a correct top-1 relative to Base, and 392 the other way. The examples are not hand-picked: from each group we drew a random sample (seed 0) of queries with at most 14 words, so that the text fits in the figure, and we show the first four draws of each.

sections.heading: Corrections.
sections.text: In Figure 5 (Section 4.6 ), Base ranks the correct image second or third, and Full moves it to first. Besides the sandwich and desk examples discussed there, Base prefers a different child batting in a cage for the baseball query and a dark Gothic cathedral for a query about a beige building. In both cases the correct image’s captions name the missing detail, and the consensus term recovers it.

sections.heading: Failures.
sections.text: Figure 6 shows the reverse case, in which Base ranks the correct image first and Full demotes it to second. Here the query is generic (“a double decker bus driving down a street”, “a skateboarder does a trick at an indoor skate park”), and the distractor that rises to the top is an equally valid match: another double-decker bus, another tennis player waiting for a serve, another skateboarder in a skate park. When several images fit the query equally well, the captions of a distractor can agree with the query as closely as those of the correct image, and the consensus term no longer separates them. Several of these errors therefore appear to be false negatives of the single-positive evaluation. Figure 6: Text-to-image queries where support captions hurt the ranking, drawn at random from all such queries. The correct image (green) drops from rank 1 under Base to rank 2 under Full; in each case the new top-ranked image is also a plausible match for the generic query.

Retrieval benchmarks and many collections attach several captions to each picture, yet dual encoders still judge every image-caption pair in isolation. We ask what these neighboring captions contribute when a frozen encoder consults them at inference time. Fusing image similarity with similarity to an image’s own captions improves text-to-image R@1 by 3.4 to 16.8 points across nine frozen encoders when the captions come from the same annotators as the queries. The gain falls to 1.9 to 7.2 points when an off-the-shelf captioner writes them, and to at most one point when they come from a different annotation source; a paraphrase-trained text encoder strengthens the text side further. A natural refinement, scoring the part of the image that the captions leave unexplained, appears to add much more under a leave-one-out evaluation. We show that this advantage arises because the correct candidate’s supports are built differently from those of the negative candidates, with set size and query removal each contributing about half, and that under a fixed support index the residual reduces to a reweighting of what the captions already provide. On compositional benchmarks, the captions help by matching candidates to human descriptions of the image, without improving image-text grounding. The code is available at: https://github.com/nhatkhangcs/clip_consensus 1 Introduction Dual encoders such as CLIP ( Radford et al., 2021 ) and SigLIP ( Zhai et al., 2023 ) map images and text into a shared embedding space and retrieve by cosine similarity. This simple design supports zero-shot classification and image-text retrieval at scale, and later work has improved it through alternative losses, data curation, and scaling ( Cherti et al., 2023 ; Xu et al., 2024 ; Gadre et al., 2023 ; Fang et al., 2024 ; Sun et al., 2023 ) . At retrieval time, however, each image is still represented by a single vector, and each image-caption pair is scored in isolation. Many image collections offer more than the image itself. COCO and Flickr30K attach five human captions to every image ( Lin et al., 2014 ; Young et al., 2014 ) , and curated repositories often store alt text, descriptions, or other metadata alongside each picture. These captions describe overlapping but non-identical aspects of the scene: some content is mentioned by every annotator, while other details appear in only one caption ( Plummer et al., 2017 ) . Standard image-text benchmarks use them as queries or training targets, but not as evidence when a candidate image is scored. Figure 1: With image similarity alone, the query is closest to a distractor. Adding the consensus of the correct image’s own captions recovers the correct match. Figure 1 illustrates why these captions can help. For the query “A person in a grass field flying a kite,” image similarity alone prefers a photo of a person reaching for a Frisbee in tall grass, whereas the captions of the correct image, which describe people flying kites on a lawn, lie much closer to the query than its image embedding does. Using candidate-side text in this way is a form of database-side augmentation and late fusion, long used in instance retrieval ( Chum et al., 2007 ; Arandjelović and Zisserman, 2012 ) , document expansion ( Nogueira et al., 2019 ) , and retrieval over multimodal candidates ( Wei et al., 2024 ) . We do not propose it as a new method. Instead, we ask how much it actually helps frozen dual encoders, and how to evaluate it without leakage. We study a simple scorer: the support captions of each candidate image are averaged into a consensus direction, the image embedding is decomposed into a component along this direction and a residual, and the query is scored by a weighted sum of image, consensus, and residual similarity, with only two fusion weights tuned. Evaluating such a scorer requires care. In multi-caption benchmarks, the query is usually one of the correct image’s own captions, so it must be excluded from that image’s supports. A natural remedy, leave-one-out (LOO), removes the query from the correct candidate only. Under LOO, the full scorer outperforms a tuned base-plus-consensus scorer by 5.3 to 8.1 points in image-to-text R@1 on COCO. Under a fixed support index, in which every candidate uses the same supports regardless of the query, this advantage falls to at most 0.7 points. A size-matched variant of LOO, in which every negative also drops one caption, recovers about half of the gap, so set size and query removal each account for roughly half of the inflation. The support captions themselves, however, help every encoder we evaluate. Our contributions are as follows. • A leakage-free protocol. We evaluate candidate-side captions under a fixed support index, with every scorer tuned on the same objective and image-clustered bootstrap intervals, and release it as a standalone evaluation script. • An account of the LOO pitfall. We show that LOO inflates the apparent benefit of a residual term derived from the same captions. A size-matched LOO, a random-support control, and an algebraic analysis show that the residual reduces to a candidate-dependent reweighting of image and consensus similarity, which yields at most a small text-to-image gain. • Measurements of when candidate-side text helps. Text-to-image R@1 improves by 3.4 to 16.8 points with same-source human captions across nine frozen encoders, by 1.9 to 7.2 points with captions from an off-the-shelf captioner across six, and by at most one point with captions from a different annotation source across four. A paraphrase-trained text encoder strengthens the text side, the gains persist under corrected COCO positives, and on SugarCrepe and ARO they come from text-to-text matching against human descriptions of the image, not from better image-text grounding. 2 Related Work Image-text dual encoders. CLIP and ALIGN train dual encoders to align matched image-caption pairs in a shared embedding space, enabling zero-shot classification and image-text retrieval ( Radford et al., 2021 ; Jia et al., 2021 ) . Later work improves this recipe through scaling ( Cherti et al., 2023 ) , the pairwise sigmoid loss of SigLIP ( Zhai et al., 2023 ; Tschannen et al., 2025 ) , data curation in MetaCLIP, DataComp, and DFN ( Xu et al., 2024 ; Gadre et al., 2023 ; Fang et al., 2024 ) , and improved training as in EVA-CLIP ( Sun et al., 2023 ) . Retrieval has also been improved with hard negatives ( Faghri et al., 2018 ) , region-word or token-level interaction ( Lee et al., 2018 ; Yao et al., 2022 ) , and fusion or generative pre-training ( Li et al., 2021 ; Li et al., 2022 ; Li et al., 2023a ; Yu et al., 2022 ) . A related line questions the one-to-one image-caption assumption during training, through multiple positives ( Bulat et al., 2024 ) , generated captions ( Wang et al., 2025 ) , richer image representations ( Lavoie et al., 2024 ) , or objectives that capture more than shared information ( Dufumier et al., 2025 ) . All of these change training; we keep the encoder frozen and change only how candidates are scored. Candidate-side text and late fusion. Augmenting each database item with related content is an established retrieval technique. In instance retrieval, average query expansion and database-side augmentation replace an item’s descriptor with the mean of its neighbors ( Chum et al., 2007 ; Arandjelović and Zisserman, 2012 ) ; in text retrieval, document expansion appends predicted queries to each document ( Nogueira et al., 2019 ) . Benchmarks with multimodal candidates, such as M-BEIR, score image-text pairs by fusing image and text similarities ( Wei et al., 2024 ) , and ECO re-ranks captions of a fixed image by their agreement with other captions ( Jeong et al., 2024 ) . The scorer we study applies the same idea to frozen vision-language retrieval, with each candidate’s own captions as the added text. Our focus is therefore not the fusion itself but how much it helps, which text encoder suits the text side, from sparse BM25 ( Robertson and Zaragoza, 2009 ) to sentence encoders ( Reimers and Gurevych, 2019 ; Wang et al., 2022 ; Li et al., 2023b ) , and how to evaluate it without leakage. Inference-time score normalization. Cross-modal retrieval can also be improved at inference time without any metadata, by normalizing scores against other queries. Inverted softmax ( Smith et al., 2017 ) and dual softmax ( Cheng et al., 2021 ) renormalize over the evaluated query set, and QB-Norm uses a separate query bank to reduce hubness ( Bogolin et al., 2022 ) . We compare against these methods to separate gains that require captions from gains that any normalization provides. Evaluation of image-text retrieval. COCO and Flickr30K pair each image with five captions ( Lin et al., 2014 ; Young et al., 2014 ) , and Flickr30K Entities links entity mentions across them ( Plummer et al., 2017 ) ; Localized Narratives add a second, independent description of the same images ( Pont-Tuset et al., 2020 ) . Single-positive COCO evaluation misses many valid matches, which CxC and ECCV Caption correct with additional human and machine-verified positives ( Parekh et al., 2021 ; Chun et al., 2022 ) . Compositional benchmarks such as Winoground, ARO, CREPE, and SugarCrepe test whether models distinguish captions with the same words in different structures ( Thrush et al., 2022 ; Yuksekgonul et al., 2023 ; Ma et al., 2023 ; Hsieh et al., 2023 ) ; Hsieh et al. (2023) show that blind text models solve many earlier benchmarks. We follow this concern and pair every compositional result with blind baselines that never see the image. 3 Methodology Figure 2: Overview of the consensus-residual scorer. Make support sets independent of the query. Any construction that treats the positive candidate differently from the negatives can inflate a scorer’s apparent benefit. Leave-one-out differs in both set size and content, and the image-to-text gain of 5.3 to 8.1 points it produces shrinks to at most 0.7 points under a fixed support index. Where LOO cannot be avoided, a size-matched variant at least removes the set-size effect. Compare new terms against tuned simpler scorers. The residual term looked essential until base-plus-consensus was tuned under the same protocol and objective. Its algebraic form then explained why: it only reweights similarities that the simpler scorer already uses. Each ablated variant should therefore be retuned, not evaluated with the weights of the full model. Choose the text side deliberately. A dual encoder’s own text tower is not trained for paraphrase similarity, and a sentence encoder over the same captions outperformed it for all six encoders. Which encoder reads the supports is a design decision in its own right, not a detail inherited from the image model. Report where the supports come from. How much the supports help depends on how closely they resemble the queries. Same-source human captions give the largest gains, generated captions recover part of them, and captions from another annotation source add almost nothing. A result obtained with same-source supports therefore overstates what to expect in deployment, where queries and metadata are seldom written alike. Calibrate to support quality. Weights tuned on clean supports can push retrieval below the image-only baseline when supports are noisy, whereas in our tests weights retuned for the noise level kept it at or above Base. Fusion weights should match the support quality expected at deployment. Pair compositional results with blind baselines. A language model that never sees the image solves ARO-Order, so improvements on it say nothing about grounding. Reporting blind and random-support references next to any scorer that uses text shows what a gain actually measures. 6 Conclusion We asked how much the captions attached to database images help frozen dual encoders at retrieval time, and how to measure it without leakage. Under a fixed support index, fusing image similarity with similarity to an image’s own captions improves text-to-image R@1 for every encoder we tested. The gain is largest when the captions share an annotation source with the queries, about half as large when an off-the-shelf captioner writes them, and close to zero when they come from a different source. The text encoder deserves as much care as the fusion: a paraphrase-trained sentence encoder over the same captions outperforms each dual encoder’s own text tower. The residual term that motivated our decomposition adds little. Its large image-to-text advantage under leave-one-out evaluation arises because the positive’s supports are built differently from those of the negatives, with set size and query removal each explaining part of the gap; under a fixed index, it reduces to a reweighting of image and consensus similarity. On compositional benchmarks, the gains come from matching candidates against human descriptions of the image, not from better grounding, and ARO can be solved without the image. We release the fixed-support-index protocol so that future work on candidate-side text can be compared on equal terms. Limitations Our setting assumes that each database image comes with descriptive text. We evaluate human captions from COCO and Flickr30K, Localized Narratives, and captions generated by Qwen2.5-VL, but not naturally occurring metadata such as alt text, Wikipedia descriptions, or product titles, whose relation to the queries may differ. Because the scorer sees text that image-only retrieval does not, comparisons with Base measure the value of that text, not an improvement of the encoder. The fusion weights are tuned on labeled COCO images. They transfer to Flickr30K, but both datasets consist of short, crowd-sourced English captions written under similar guidelines, and we have not evaluated other languages or domains. With generated supports, the captioner is itself a strong vision model, so part of the gain may stem from its visual knowledge and not from the text alone. The gains shrink as the base model becomes stronger, to about one point for BLIP-2 with ITM re-ranking, and they decrease with fewer supports per image (Appendix B.4 ). Under the fixed support index, image-to-text R@1 has a single correct caption per query and is not comparable to standard five-positive results, so we treat it as a diagnostic. Several analyses (cross-source supports, fusion rules, residual variants, and the random-support control) were run on a subset of encoders. Finally, ARO can be solved by a blind language model, so among our compositional benchmarks only SugarCrepe speaks to grounding, and there the captions help through text matching instead of through the image.
